newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - EMU woes leave BTP vols well-supported.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - EMU woes leave BTP vols well-supported.

text.p: Increasing uncertainty over Italy's future in European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will keep implied volatility of Italian BTP options firm, traders on the LIFFE floor said on Wednesday.

In the last week of January, at-the-money volatility fell as low as 6.9 percent -- remarkable not just because the market is more used to a double-digit level, but also because it was trading within one percentage point of Bund option volatility.
"We had a situation where BTP options were at 6.9 percent and Bund vols were at 5.9 percent, which was crazy," said Lauren O'Hara, manager at the HSBC futures desk on the LIFFE floor.
"We advised people to sell Bund vol and buy BTP vol, and look where we are now," she said.

June at-the-money BTP volatility was trading at 8.25 percent by 1130 GMT, after ending Tuesday around 8.28 percent. June Bund volatility meanwhile was at 5.7 percent. Traders said the euphoria appeared to have got out of hand, as investors were carried away by the idea that EMU was a one-way bet. Italian futures soared to a record high last month at 132.38. March futures are currently trading at 130.39, up 67 basis points, while June was up 0.57 at 129.75.
Even before European Union officials said on Wednesday that a plan to delay Italy's membership of a single currency was under consideration, implied volatility started to creep up.

A trader at a U.S. bank on the LIFFE floor said volatility had dipped down as low as 8.12 percent, but had attracted interest at those lower levels. Traders said many investors were looking for dips in volatility as a buying opportunity.
"If it gets anywhere down to 7.5, it's a definite buy," said a trader at a British brokerage.
The most notable trade was June call spread at the 129.00, 131.00 strikes which was done in lots of 1,000.
"Call buying in June, and puts and put spreads in March were popular today," said the trader, adding that volume was lighter than during the previous session.
O'Hara said volatility was likely to remain well-bid as there was a reluctance to sell it down.
"The thing about BTPs is that when they turn, they turn fast," she said.
